primary_claim: Systematic analysis of 6,390 agent evaluation transcripts across nine anonymized frontier models revealed quality issues -- hard refusals, low tool-call compliance, and task resignation -- that undermine the validity of pass-rate-based capability claims, with one model (B4) failing to genuinely attempt at least 30% of its tasks due to refusals.

effect.metric: proportion of transcripts affected by hard refusal / non-engagement
effect.value: ~30% of B4's transcripts consisted almost entirely of refusal text ('I'm sorry, but I can't comply with that')

contradicts_or_qualifies: Pass@k rates alone, the main statistic AISI reports in pre-deployment testing, are insufficient to characterize agent capability because of bugs, under-elicitation, and refusal-driven non-engagement
stated_future_work: Developing better protocols and tools for observing and interrogating transcripts
Cross-task studies of model activity to reveal 'bugs' in AI models over time
Conceptually analysing the desirable and undesirable properties of agent transcripts
Analysing the causal structure of commentary and reasoning (why/what-if questions about agent behaviour)
limitations_stated: Manual review lacked a tighter protocol for recording feature presence/absence and frequency
No settled definition of what counts as an 'issue' in a transcript
Only a rough assessment of the extent of issues investigated, not full-coverage scanning
Scanning approach was rudimentary (message-level, closed label set, spot-checked rather than statistically validated)
Analysis focused on capability-claim validity rather than general understanding of agent behaviour
quote: B4 did not engage with the task in at least 30% of its task attempts. This was a serious fault in our results that affected the capability claims we could make for B4.
